body:
The emergence of the Maitrakas

The Maitrakas established a regional kingdom in Saurashtra during the political changes that followed the decline of Gupta imperial authority. Their capital was Vallabhi, near present-day Vallabhipur in Bhavnagar district.

The dynasty emerged in the late 5th century CE and remained politically important until the later 8th century CE. Its history is known especially through Sanskrit inscriptions on copper plates, many of which record land grants.

Bhatarka and the military background

Bhatarka, also recorded as Bhatakka in early dynastic accounts, is regarded as the founder of the Maitraka line. He held the title senapati, meaning military commander.

This origin is important because it shows how military leadership could become the foundation of a new regional ruling family. The early Maitrakas did not immediately present themselves as rulers entirely free from higher authority. Their records indicate changing degrees of royal status and acknowledgement of overlords.

Bhatarka is often described in brief historical accounts as a general who gained power after the decline of the Guptas. The evidence establishes his military title, but the precise identity of the earliest Maitrakas' overlord is uncertain. Their origin should therefore not be reduced to a claim that every early Maitraka ruler was an independent Gupta governor.

Important early rulers and titles

Early Maitraka inscriptions preserve titles that help explain the growth of the dynasty's political authority.

  • Bhatarka: Founder of the line, described as senapati or military commander.
  • Dharasena I: An early ruler who also bore the title senapati.
  • Dronasimha: Used the title maharaja, meaning king.
  • Dhruvasena I: Bore the title mahasamanta-maharaja, indicating the status of a major subordinate ruler or vassal king.

A samanta was a subordinate chief or ruler who acknowledged a superior political authority and could be expected to provide assistance, tribute or military support. The term mahasamanta indicated an important subordinate ruler. The presence of such titles explains why the rise of the Maitrakas was a gradual political development rather than an immediate transformation into a large independent empire.

Important rulers of the 7th century

Shiladitya I

Shiladitya I was an important Maitraka ruler of the early 7th century. His reign belongs to a period when the dynasty's political authority and religious endowments became more prominent. The name Shiladitya later appeared repeatedly among Maitraka rulers.

Dhruvasena II and Harshavardhana

Dhruvasena II ruled Vallabhi around the middle of the 7th century CE and was a contemporary of Harshavardhana, the powerful ruler based in northern India. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang visited Vallabhi around 640 CE and provides information about the region.

Historical accounts suggest a close political connection between Dhruvasena II and Harsha, possibly reinforced by marriage. The central prelims distinction is that Dhruvasena II was a Maitraka ruler of Vallabhi, whereas Harshavardhana was the ruler associated with Thanesar and Kanauj.

Dharasena IV

Dharasena IV, who ruled in the middle of the 7th century CE, adopted elevated royal titles, including maharajadhiraja, meaning king of great kings, and chakravartin, a title expressing an ideal of extensive sovereign authority.

Royal titles show how a king presented his authority. A title such as chakravartin does not, by itself, establish the exact geographical extent of every territory he controlled.

The later Maitrakas and decline

Later Maitraka rulers continued to use the name Shiladitya. Copper-plate grants demonstrate that the dynasty remained active into the 8th century CE; known Maitraka records extend to approximately 766 CE.

Maitraka power ended in the later 8th century amid conflicts involving neighbouring political forces and incursions into western India. Arab raids are frequently connected with the final period of Vallabhi, but the precise circumstances of the dynasty's collapse are not established by a single uncontested account. It is therefore more accurate to remember the late 8th-century decline than to assign the entire fall to one certain event.

Prelims focus

  • Bhatarka: Founder of the Maitraka dynasty and holder of the title senapati.
  • Vallabhi: Capital of the Maitrakas in Saurashtra.
  • Dronasimha: Associated with the title maharaja.
  • Dhruvasena I: Associated with the title mahasamanta-maharaja.
  • Dhruvasena II: Contemporary of Harshavardhana and associated with Xuanzang's visit around 640 CE.
  • Dharasena IV: Associated with elevated imperial titles in the middle of the 7th century.
  • Trap: The Maitraka ruler Shiladitya I must not be confused with Harshavardhana, who also used the name Shiladitya.

[Annette Schmiedchen, Maitrakas, The Encyclopedia of Ancient History: Asia and Africa, dynastic history and discussion of royal titles, first published 2021; NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts-I, New Empires and Kingdoms, printed pp. 114–117, background on regional rulers and samantas; Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency, vol. 1, part 1, History of Gujarat, Chapter VIII, section on Dharasena IV; online sources consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Maitraka titles move from military command through kingship and subordinate rule to Dharasena IV's elevated claims of sovereignty.
pictures.caption: Early Maitraka titles reveal the dynasty's changing political status.

title: The Maitrakas of Vallabhi: Origin, Rulers and Political Development

body:
How Maitraka rule was administered

The Maitraka kingdom was governed through the authority of its rulers and the work of officials who dealt with regional administration, revenue and royal orders. Agricultural villages formed an important economic foundation, while Vallabhi served as the principal political centre.

Land revenue and other dues helped support royal authority. The state could also use land and revenue rights to reward or support individuals and religious institutions. Such grants were recorded so that the recipient's claim could be recognised.

Maitraka inscriptions mention different kinds of territorial units, including grama, meaning village, and vishaya, commonly used for a district or territorial division. Other terms, such as bhukti, also appear. Their precise use could vary, so every ancient administrative term should not be forced into one unchanging modern hierarchy.

Copper-plate charters

The most characteristic documents of Maitraka administration are Sanskrit copper-plate charters. A copper-plate charter was an inscribed record of a royal grant, commonly involving a plot of land, a village or specified rights over revenue.

A typical royal grant could identify the donor, the recipient, the donated property and the conditions attached to the gift. Some records also describe the ruling family and praise the reigning king.

Why a ruler made a land grant

Royal grants served both religious and administrative purposes. A grant to a Brahmana could support the recipient's livelihood and religious duties. A grant to a Buddhist monastery could provide resources for the institution's maintenance and for the community living there.

The recipient did not necessarily receive every imaginable right over the land. Some grants conveyed particular revenue privileges or exemptions, while others contained different conditions. The exact rights depended on the charter.

Agrahara

An agrahara was land granted to a Brahmana, commonly accompanied by exemptions from specified dues or rights to receive certain revenues. The term does not mean that all inhabitants of the village necessarily became free from every obligation.

Shaiva rulers and diverse religious patronage

The Maitrakas provide an important example of the difference between a ruler's personal religious affiliation and the institutions that received royal support.

Most Maitraka kings described themselves as devoted to Shiva. A common royal epithet was paramamaheshvara, indicating strong devotion to Shiva. Yet the surviving grants show substantial patronage of both Brahmanas and Buddhist monasteries.

This is not contradictory. A ruler could identify with a particular religious tradition while granting resources to people or institutions belonging to other traditions. Such grants also maintained relationships with learned communities and established institutions within the kingdom.

Religious distinctions among the Maitrakas

  • Shaivism: The dominant religious identification expressed in Maitraka royal titles.
  • Vaishnavism: Dhruvasena I is identified in records as a devotee of Vishnu.
  • Sun worship: Dharapatta is associated with devotion to the sun.
  • Buddhism: The later known religious designation of Guhasena identifies him as a Buddhist lay follower; royal grants also supported Buddhist monasteries.
  • Jainism: Vallabhi was important in Jain literary tradition, but this must be distinguished from the documented pattern of Maitraka royal land grants.

The surviving Maitraka charters predominantly record grants to Brahmanas and Buddhist institutions. Although Jainism has a major place in Gujarat's history, presently identified Maitraka royal grants do not establish a comparable programme of land endowments to Jain institutions.

Why these grants matter

The copper plates show that political authority, agricultural revenue and religious life were closely connected. Villages produced resources; royal orders could assign some of those resources to particular recipients; and the beneficiaries used the resulting income for their activities.

They also show that the Maitraka kingdom supported institutions beyond the royal court. The growth of monasteries and learned communities at Vallabhi was connected with the wider economic resources of the region.

Prelims focus

  • Maitraka administrative records: Predominantly Sanskrit copper-plate charters.
  • Grama: Village; vishaya: Territorial division or district.
  • Agrahara: Land grant associated with a Brahmana recipient.
  • Paramamaheshvara: Royal title expressing devotion to Shiva.
  • Maitraka patronage: Especially important for Brahmanas and Buddhist monasteries.
  • Dhruvasena I: Associated with Vaishnavism; Dharapatta: Associated with sun worship.
  • Trap: A Shaiva royal title does not mean that a ruler supported only Shaiva religious institutions.

[Annette Schmiedchen, Maitrakas, The Encyclopedia of Ancient History: Asia and Africa, discussion of Sanskrit charters, religious titles and endowments, first published 2021; NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Kings, Farmers and Towns, printed pp. 40–41, Land Grants and New Rural Elites; NCERT, Class 7, Our Pasts-II, New Kings and Kingdoms, printed pp. 17–20, Administration and Land Grants; online source consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A Maitraka ruler issues a charter authorising a beneficiary, while village cultivation supplies resources for the grant’s stated purpose.
pictures.caption: Land grants connected royal authority, village resources and religious institutions.

title: Maitraka Administration, Copper-Plate Grants and Religious Patronage

body:
Vallabhi's importance beyond politics

Vallabhi was the capital of the Maitrakas, but its importance was not limited to government. During the early-medieval period it became a prominent centre of religious learning, scholarly activity and cultural exchange.

Its position in Saurashtra connected it with communities in western India and with routes used by merchants and travellers. Religious institutions received resources from rulers and other supporters, allowing communities of teachers and students to develop.

The meaning of Vallabhi University

Vallabhi is commonly described as an ancient university. In this context, the term refers to an important centre of advanced learning associated especially with Buddhist monasteries. It should not be imagined as a modern university operating under a single present-day administrative or degree system.

Monasteries, or viharas, provided a setting in which monks could reside, study, discuss religious teachings and receive instruction. Learning also included intellectual disciplines needed for understanding and debating ideas, such as grammar, reasoning and philosophical discussion.

Vallabhi attracted scholarly attention because it formed part of a wider network of recognised places of advanced learning in India.

Xuanzang's account

The Chinese Buddhist pilgrim Xuanzang, also known as Hiuen Tsang, visited Vallabhi around 640 CE, during the period of Maitraka rule.

His account describes a substantial Buddhist monastic community in the Vallabhi region. He reports approximately 100 monasteries and 6,000 monks. These figures are part of a historical traveller's description of the region, not a modern census or an independently verified count of students enrolled in one institution.

When using Xuanzang's figures, retain their context: approximately 100 monasteries and 6,000 monks in the Vallabhi region. They do not establish that 6,000 students attended a single modern-style campus.

Yijing and the comparison with Nalanda

The Chinese Buddhist scholar and traveller Yijing, also known as I-Tsing, wrote in the later 7th century CE about Buddhist education in India.

He identified Vallabhi and Nalanda as 2 especially important centres of advanced Buddhist learning. Nalanda was located in Magadha, in present-day Bihar, while Vallabhi was located in Saurashtra, Gujarat.

The comparison shows that major centres of Buddhist scholarship existed in different parts of the subcontinent. Nalanda was not the only important institution of advanced Buddhist learning.

Yijing's account does not establish that he personally visited Vallabhi. He travelled in India and wrote about Vallabhi's standing as a centre of learning, but a description of an institution must not automatically be treated as proof of a visit to that institution.

Vallabhi and the Shvetambara Jain tradition

Vallabhi also has an important place in the literary history of Shvetambara Jainism. Jain tradition associates the city with the collection, arrangement and writing down of important Jain Agamas, the religious texts transmitted within the Shvetambara tradition.

The work is traditionally associated with the Jain teacher Devardhigani Kshamashramana. Accounts commonly place it around the 5th or 6th century CE, but the historical evidence for the precise date and details of the council is not conclusive.

It is therefore appropriate to remember Vallabhi's association with the Shvetambara Jain canon without treating one disputed council date as a certain fact.

The Buddhist monastic learning centre at Vallabhi and the Jain tradition of textual compilation at Vallabhi are related through their location and cultural environment, but they are not the same institution or the same religious event.

Cultural significance

Vallabhi's history demonstrates the coexistence of different intellectual and religious traditions in early-medieval Gujarat. Its rulers were predominantly identified with Shaivism, Buddhist institutions received significant support, and the city was remembered in Jain literary tradition.

This combination made Vallabhi an important regional centre for political administration, religious patronage and scholarship.

Prelims focus

  • Vallabhi: Maitraka capital and important early-medieval learning centre in Saurashtra.
  • Xuanzang: Visited Vallabhi around 640 CE.
  • Xuanzang's reported figures: Approximately 100 monasteries and 6,000 monks in the Vallabhi region.
  • Yijing: Compared Vallabhi and Nalanda as important centres of Buddhist learning in the later 7th century.
  • Nalanda: Associated with Magadha in present-day Bihar.
  • Shvetambara Jain tradition: Associates Vallabhi with the compilation of Agamas under Devardhigani Kshamashramana.
  • Trap: Yijing's discussion of Vallabhi does not establish a personal visit, and the Jain council should not be confused with the Buddhist learning centre.

[Annette Schmiedchen, Maitrakas, The Encyclopedia of Ancient History: Asia and Africa, discussion of Buddhist monasteries, royal endowments and Yijing, first published 2021; H. G. Shastri, Valabhi Vidyapith, Samipya, vol. 8, 1991–1992, printed pp. 17–18; Royce Wiles, The Dating of the Jaina Councils, in Studies in Jaina History and Culture: Disputes and Dialogues, pp. 61–85, especially pp. 61–65; online sources consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Buddhist monasteries at Vallabhi supported teaching, study and scholarly discussion.

title: Vallabhi as a Centre of Learning: Buddhism and Jain Literary Tradition
